personas.story: Ana runs bot management for a CDN. A retail customer wants shopping agents in and scrapers out. She turns on TAP verification: the edge reads Signature-Input, checks the tag, the 8-minute window and the nonce, fetches the key for keyid and verifies the signature. On day one the dashboard shows a spike of requests tagged web-bot-auth from an agent that copied Cloudflare's example, and she routes them to the normal bot policy. She also notices the Visa key store holds one RSA key, so she asks Visa how production keys reach her edge. Until she gets an answer, she keeps the rule in log-only mode.

personas.story: Malik leads payments at a fashion retailer. Agents were tripping the bot wall at checkout, so he asks the CDN to let TAP-signed requests through. His team then builds the merchant side: compare each body object's nonce with the header nonce, verify the signatures, and decrypt the payload. The ID Token does not give emails in the clear, so they build a table that maps obfuscated values to existing accounts. Legal asks who carries a dispute on an agent order. He finds that Visa's rules make the cardholder answer, within Visa's system, for an Agentic Payment Provider's actions but call nothing a liability shift. He books the orders as ordinary tokenized card-not-present sales for now.

personas.story: Priya builds the shopping agent for an AI assistant. After VIC onboarding, her agent signs each product page request with agent-browser-auth and each checkout with agent-payer-auth, inside an 8-minute window. Checkout also needs the two signed objects, and her first build fails at a merchant because the merchant joined the fields in a different order. With no test vector in the specification, she agrees a byte format with that merchant and files the question with Visa. The user's passkey approval sits in VIC, so her agent never asks for a card number.

personas.story: Lena runs digital fraud at a European bank in the Agentic Ready program. Her cardholders now link cards to shopping agents: VIC runs step-up verification, the user sets up a passkey, and the agent gets its own token. When a purchase arrives she sees a token transaction, not the merchant's TAP check, so she relies on Visa's signals. A customer disputes a hotel booking made by an agent. The passkey approval of the Payment Instruction helps. Within Visa's system the cardholder answers for what an Agentic Payment Provider does, but Visa's rules yield to applicable law such as PSD2. The case runs under the usual dispute rules.

personas.story: Tom works on the agentic commerce team at Visa. TAP launched on 2025-10-14 with twelve partners and Cloudflare, and by 2026-07-02 agents completed live purchases at named European merchants. His inbox holds the hard questions: why the key store has one sandbox RSA key, why the examples cannot verify, and why community fixes sit unmerged. He also follows the IETF Web Bot Auth draft, which differs from TAP in tags and key discovery. He drafts a plan for a versioned specification with test vectors and a public directory.

personas.story: Sam tunes fraud rules for an acquirer's merchants. A valid TAP signature proves an approved agent signed this host and path in the last 8 minutes, but nothing about the method or body. He scores TAP as one strong signal among others, keeps nonce records so a copied request fails, and refuses payment containers that fail verification. When a merchant asks to use unverified consumer data to skip login, he says no. He also flags the credential hash: without a stated salt, the hash of a card number and a three-digit code is weak.
